title: Nontrivial agnostic membership-query learning of \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\)
formal: Can polynomial-size constant-depth modular circuits be agnostically learned under uniform inputs using membership queries in time \(2^n/n^{\omega(1)}\)? Precisely, for every fixed depth bound \(d\ge1\), fixed modulus \(m\ge2\), and fixed integer size exponent \(k\ge1\), do there exist one uniform randomized oracle Turing machine \(A_{d,m,k}\), an integer \(n_0\), and a saving function \(\sigma:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[0,\infty)\) such that \(\sigma(n)/\log_2 n\to\infty\) and the following holds? For every \(n\ge n_0\) and every joint distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\times\{-1,+1\}\) whose first marginal is uniform, \(A_{d,m,k}\), given \(1^n\) and the conditional-label oracle described below, runs in worst-case time at most \(2^{n-\sigma(n)}\) and outputs a hypothesis \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr\left[\operatorname{corr}_D(h)\ge \max_{c\in\operatorname{ACC}_{d,m,k}(n)}\operatorname{corr}_D(c)-2^{-n^{99/100}}\right]\ge\frac13,\qquad \operatorname{corr}_D(g):=\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim D}[g(x)y].\] All machine coins and oracle responses are included in this probability. The success constant \(1/3\) is the literal consequence of the source’s full-learning convention \(1-\delta\) and its assignment \(\delta=2/3\); it is recorded explicitly rather than silently exchanged with the separate weak-learning convention.

source_formulation.text: Is there a nontrivial agnostic membership-query learner for ACC⁰, even with uniformly distributed unlabelled examples?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

why: Constant-depth circuits with modular gates are a central boundary class in circuit complexity. The question asks whether their predictive structure can be exploited even when labels need not come from that class and the learner may choose its queries. The requested saving must beat every fixed polynomial factor relative to the exponential scale while retaining the source’s high-accuracy guarantee.
status_note: Explicitly open in the checked ALT 2024 source, including the easier realizable uniform-input case. The completed statement preserves the selected agnostic version and the source’s fixed epsilon=2^(-n^0.99), superlogarithmic saving and literal delta=2/3 assignment (success 1/3); its separate weak-learner display has success 2/3. The prime-modulus multiplicative-error result does not match. Live version history and bounded later-work checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution, so current status remains uncertain.

The source gives full agnostic nontrivial-time algorithms for restricted circuit classes and explicitly identifies ACC⁰ as beyond the known uniform-input learning frontier.

category_assignment.reason: The requested algorithm is agnostic learning of a circuit class.

importance.reason: A foundational algorithmic boundary for ACC⁰, connecting expressive constant-depth modular circuits with strong agnostic query learning. The source identifies the class as beyond the current learning frontier even in the easier realizable uniform-input setting.

sentences: The card asks whether constant-depth modular circuits admit agnostic membership-query learning with a superpolynomial-factor saving over exponential time.
Inputs are uniform, labels may be arbitrary and stochastic, and each chosen query receives a fresh conditional label.
The target keeps the source’s exponentially small correlation slack and its literal one-third full-learning success guarantee.
Known positive results restrict the circuit class or relax the optimum-error comparison and do not establish the full ACC⁰ target.
A Lean answer must prove the complete uniform algorithmic assertion or its unconditional negation under these exact resource and accuracy conventions.

definitions:
An \(\operatorname{ACC}_{d,m,k}(n)\) circuit is a finite acyclic circuit with \(n\) input bits, constants, unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates, one-input NOT gates, and unbounded-fan-in \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gates. A \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gate returns one exactly when the number of its one-valued inputs is divisible by \(m\). There are at most \(d\) gates along each input-to-output path and at most \(n^k\) internal gates and wires in total. Its output bit is converted to \(-1,+1\) by \(b\mapsto2b-1\). Fix an effective binary encoding of gates and their ordered incoming wires. These fixed-depth, fixed-modulus, polynomial-size classes give the usual \(\mathrm{ACC}^0\) target when the fixed parameters vary. Gate-count versus wire-count conventions change polynomial size exponents only; the question quantifies over every exponent. The parameters are fixed before input length and may determine the learner and its saving; neither depth nor modulus grows with \(n\). Hidden comparator circuits may be chosen independently at different lengths and need not form a uniformly constructible family. No target circuit description is given to the learner.

The joint distribution \(D\) is otherwise arbitrary. For each chosen query \(z\in\{0,1\}^n\), the oracle returns one fresh label sampled from \(D(Y\mid X=z)\), independently of its earlier samples conditional on the submitted queries. Queries may adapt to previous answers, and repeated queries need not agree. The uniform marginal gives every \(z\) positive probability, so all conditional label distributions are defined. Labels may be deterministic, stochastic, noisy, or inconsistent with every comparator circuit; no realizability promise is made. The learner knows the uniform marginal and can itself draw uniform inputs. It has no sampler description for the label probabilities, equivalence oracle, circuit advice, or oracle access to an optimal comparator. Correlation lies in \([-1,1]\), and the maximum exists because the comparator set is finite and nonempty. For \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued functions, zero-one error equals \((1-\operatorname{corr})/2\); thus the displayed correlation slack is excess prediction error at most \(2^{-n^{99/100}}/2\), rather than a multiplicative approximation to optimum error.

The output is a finite description of an ordinary Boolean circuit with AND, OR and NOT gates, interpreted as \(h:\{0,1\}^n\to\{-1,+1\}\). The hypothesis need not be an ACC circuit, have depth \(d\), or have size \(n^k\); this is improper learning. Its description is counted in the learner’s running time, and it is evaluated without further training queries. Using ordinary finite circuits makes the usual effectively evaluable hypothesis convention explicit. All query writing and reading, fair random bits, bit computation and output writing count toward worst-case running time; one submitted label is one oracle response, and the oracle’s internal generation cost is not charged. Consequently the number of queries is bounded by the same time. There is no real-arithmetic unit-cost computation in the learner. The exponential accuracy threshold is a mathematical success condition fixed by \(n\), not an exact irrational input that must be encoded or compared by the machine.

The expression \(2^n/n^{\omega(1)}\) means that a single learner for each fixed \((d,m,k)\) has a saving \(\sigma(n)\) whose ratio to \(\log_2 n\) tends to infinity: for every real \(B>0\), eventually \(\sigma(n)\ge B\log_2 n\). The saving is a runtime-bound witness, not an additional oracle or input. Finite exceptional lengths are allowed. A fixed-factor improvement or division by one fixed power of \(n\) is insufficient. Polynomial factors in an otherwise qualifying time can be absorbed into a smaller saving with the same limit. No efficient procedure for constructing the learner uniformly from the fixed depth, modulus and size exponent is additionally requested.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the displayed existence statement, or of its full logical negation: some fixed \((d,m,k)\) admits no uniform learner with the stated eventual superlogarithmic saving and correlation guarantee simultaneously for all uniform-marginal label distributions. A positive answer must meet the specified shrinking accuracy, the literal full-learning success constant, the conditional-query interface and worst-case total time, including a finite evaluable output. Constant-error learning, realizable-only learning, a fixed polynomial-factor saving or a multiplicative optimum-error factor does not meet this agnostic target. A lower bound against a restricted query method or a conditional cryptographic obstruction is not the unconditional negation unless the additional assumption is also proved. This is an exact asymptotic yes/no statement, not a request to approximate a numerical quantity.

context_blocks.text: Agnostic learning compares the returned predictor with the best member of a chosen circuit class, while allowing the observed labels to be generated by an arbitrary process. Membership queries let the learner choose which input is labeled; they do not reveal a target circuit or guarantee that an exact circuit representation exists. The original paper fixes both the extremely small correlation slack and the confidence parameter when defining its nontrivial-time problem.

The source explicitly states that the ACC⁰ problem is open even with uniform inputs and even without the agnostic requirement. This card retains the agnostic question selected in its title and records the source’s uniform-input version. It does not replace the comparator by only prime-modulus circuits or by a restricted family of symmetric-polynomial gates.

Carmosino–Impagliazzo–Kabanets–Kolokolova obtain quasipolynomial-time query learning for prime-modulus AC⁰[q] with a polylogarithmic multiplicative factor on optimum error. That is a meaningful earlier result, but both the restricted modulus and the multiplicative error criterion differ from full ACC⁰ agnostic learning with the additive slack specified here.

Karchmer’s positive results treat several circuit classes built from restricted low-degree threshold or symmetric-polynomial functions. Those classes include functions outside earlier families, but the published statement does not contain all polynomial-size ACC⁰ circuits. The paper separately identifies that missing full class as a frontier question.

The full-learning definition gives success at least 1−δ and then sets δ to 2/3. The separate weak-learner definition uses success at least 2/3. These are distinct displays in the source. This record preserves the literal full-learning guarantee 1/3 and marks the convention explicitly; it does not assume a typographical correction or silently use the weak definition as the target.

The original arXiv record still lists only its November 2023 version, and the checked published ALT 2024 text contains the question. Bounded later-work searches through September 2026 found no matching theorem, but that search is not a proof of continued openness. Current status is therefore recorded as uncertain.
